transcript:
Header:
Date: 2028-06-21
Start: 10:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Carlos Rivera (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood SRE Advisor), Lena Ortiz (EmberBank Head of ML), Samir Patel (EmberBank Platform), Nina Gomez (EmberBank SRE), Oliver Park (EmberBank Product)

Summary: quick sync on POC latency tuning. Reviewed this week's TTFT and streaming tests, discussed sequence length trimming and kernel choices. Agreed on next tests and to share raw traces and a benchmark spreadsheet.

Topics: TTFT (time-to-first-token), streaming vs chunked response, sequence length distribution, kernel selection and quantization, KV cache priming, 95th/99th percentile tail latency, rollout plan for Dedicated vs Hosted.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Alrigh', good morning everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — hey Lena, Samir?
[00:06] Lena Ortiz: Hey Maya, hi everyone, yep we're here.
[00:09] Samir Patel: Morning. Sorry running a tiny bit late on the network tests.
[00:12] Carlos Rivera: No worries, we'll share the traces. Objective today is to go through the TTFT numbers from last week's run and talk about kernel choices for the model, and streaming config.
[00:20] Nina Gomez: quick note: our staging env had a couple of background jobs, ignore the p99 spike at ~9:30 local, we flagged it.
[00:26] Priya Nair: Also want to double-check sequence length distributions — we've seen a lot of short queries which changes batching efficiency.
[00:33] Maya Chen: Great, so summary of the bench: with streaming enabled and our optimized kernel set (we tried aten-like fused attention variant + nv_fused), avg TTFT dropped from ~180ms to ~150ms on the 2k seq runs, and median token latency also improved about 12%. But we noticed p95 didn't move as much, still ~420ms.
[00:49] Samir Patel: Was that with KV cache warmed or cold start?
[00:52] Carlos Rivera: Cold start for that run, Samir. We did a separate primed run — when we primed KV cache the first token time improved further to ~130ms median, p95 to ~360ms. But priming requires a warm path and changes cost.
[01:06] Lena Ortiz: So tradeoff is extra priming cost vs better tail-latency. For EmberBank our SLAs care about p95.
[01:12] Maya Chen: Right. Also we tried reducing effective sequence length for batching — cutting the max from 2048 to 512 for user queries that are typically short. That improved batching efficiency and reduced queuing latency — especially with continuous batching on the Dedicated config.
[01:27] Oliver Park: Wait, if we cap at 512 what about inputs that legitimately need 2k?
[01:30] Carlos Rivera: We recommend a tiered policy: default cap 512 for front-line customers, fallback to 2048 for flagged flows. That keeps the common-case fast.
[01:37] Nina Gomez: Any impact on output quality? We worry about truncation.
[01:39] Maya Chen: We tested truncation-aware prompts and in the majority of our evals quality delta was negligible for chat-style queries. For long-document summarization we'd route to a different pipeline.
[01:46] Samir Patel: Kernel choices — you mentioned nv_fused vs aten, what was the delta?
[01:49] Carlos Rivera: nv_fused gave slightly better single-token throughput on A100-family with fp16, while aten-fused was more stable at longer sequences. The mixed approach: nv_fused for short sequences and aten-fused for long sequences gave best p50 and p95 tradeoff. We also fitted a lightweight dispatcher to pick kernel by seq len threshold at runtime.
[02:09] Priya Nair: Did you test quantized kernels? We tried int8 and saw minor quality drop but big perf wins.
[02:14] Carlos Rivera: Yes — int8 4-bit quant gave us ~20-30% lower GPU utilization per token but added jitter on some prompt types. For EmberBank's use-case we think q4f16 is promising — good perf, minimal quality regression. We'll share exact evals.
[02:27] Lena Ortiz: On streaming: we saw early bytes are good but sometimes model stalls mid-stream when the chunk size is too big.
[02:33] Maya Chen: That's expected. We tuned chunk_size down to 16 tokens and chunk_latency budget to 60ms — reduced perceived TTFT for the user. But smaller chunks increase overhead; it's a balance.
[02:45] Samir Patel: How about network overhead? We have strict egress limits.
[02:48] Maya Chen: We accounted for that — streaming with compression and fewer keep-alives helped. We'll add a config suggestion to the spreadsheet.
[02:55] Oliver Park: Any surprises in the traces?
[02:57] Carlos Rivera: One thing — kernel fallback occurs when sequence lengths spike and the dispatcher picks aten fallback which has a small recompile/hotpath cost the first time. That caused a couple small p99 blips. We can pre-warm the fallback kernel for sequences we expect.
[03:12] Nina Gomez: Is pre-warm a thing we can automate?
[03:14] Carlos Rivera: Yes, we can schedule a lightweight warm-up job that pokes the model with representative sequences. We'll include an example cron job in the repo.
[03:21] Lena Ortiz: Okay, clear. On the question of hosted vs Dedicated — any guidance on which mode to pick now?
[03:25] Maya Chen: For this stage, Dedicated gives easier kernel tuning and predictable throughput. Hosted still fine but noisy for extreme p95 guarantees. If EmberBank wants strict SLA for mission-critical flows, Dedicated reserved capacity is recommended.
[03:36] Samir Patel: We are leaning Dedicated for high-volume flows but might keep hosted for dev/test.
[03:40] Priya Nair: We also need to validate our SSO and audit log hookups before we move to Dedicated.
[03:45] Maya Chen: Understood — we've shared SOC2/ISO docs before, will re-share the compliance pack and the SAML integration guide.
[03:52] Carlos Rivera: Next technical tests we propose: 1) run p95 TTFT with KV priming across 10k queries, 2) run mixed kernel dispatcher with thresholds at 128/512/1024 and capture p50/p95/p99, 3) test q4f16 quantized run for 48-hour stability. We'll attach the exact commands to the spreadsheet.
[04:12] Lena Ortiz: That sounds good. Samir will run staging tests. We'll also provide the real sequence length histogram from production anonymized.
[04:20] Samir Patel: Yep will do, aim to get logs up by Monday.
[04:23] Maya Chen: Cool. Any final questions?
[04:26] Oliver Park: Not from product, just want the benchmark doc.
[04:29] Maya Chen: We'll send that after the call — link to the sheet: https://redwood.app/benchmarks/ember-2028 (shared). Also sending the kernel recommendation doc and cron warm-up example repo link.
[04:40] Nina Gomez: Thanks all.
[04:42] Maya Chen: Great, we'll follow up with the action items. Next sync same time next week unless anyone needs an earlier deep-dive.
[04:48] Lena Ortiz: Next week works. Thanks.

End of meeting.

Artifacts mentioned:
